ut_bluff_street_cracks.blurb: A compact sandstone cliff on the northern edge of St. George, looking south over town. Every line here is a trad climb, and the cliff is built from hand cracks, wider cracks and corners, so a rack with plenty of cams is the tool for the job. Grades run from 5.8 up to a single 5.12, but the bulk sit around 5.10, which makes it a good stop for a leader who is comfortable jamming. One route is two pitches; the rest are single pitch. It is a quick outing from town rather than a full-day destination, and the south exposure makes it a cool-season choice.

ut_chief_wall.blurb: One of the seven walls at Ruth Lake, high in the Uinta Mountains of northeast Utah at roughly 10,500 feet. Chief Wall is a newer, small cliff with mostly bolted lines and a couple of gear routes. Grades start at 5.6 and top out in the 5.11s and low 5.12s, with the largest group at 5.10, so there is something for a beginner leader and a few steps up for a stronger one. The lake basin stays mostly shady, which suits hot days, and this wall tends to be quieter than the busier Good Medicine wall nearby.
ut_chief_wall.approach: Follow the main Ruth Lake trail and, about 100 yards beyond the Haymakers and Hibernators sign, bear left onto a side path. Cross a stretch of flat rock marked with small cairns, bear left again at the next split, and climb straight to the base.

ut_pipeline_the.blurb: A long sport wall running along the left-hand side of the Left Fork in Maple Canyon, with the Pictograph Wall facing it from the other side. All twenty routes are bolted, and the grades are firmly in the intermediate-to-hard range: a couple of 5.10s, then a big block of 5.11 and 5.12 climbs. This is conglomerate cobble climbing, so expect pockets, knobs and sustained, athletic movement. It holds several of the best-rated lines in the fork, and it is not a place to start if you are still building up to 5.10.

ut_north_side.blurb: A cluster of dark, varnish-coated walls in the Garth Rocks near St. George, on the Aerial Wall. The climbing is almost all sport, plus one top rope and one trad line, and the routes are short and close to the road. Grades start at 5.6 and include a handful of easy-to-moderate lines in the 5.7 to 5.9 range, but the heaviest concentration is at 5.11, with one route up in the 5.13s. That mix suits a short session for climbers working at the 5.11 level, while newer leaders have a few warm-ups. Walk times between the walls are brief.
ut_north_side.approach: Park at the top of the airport hill, pulling off to the left, and follow the trail north along the foot of the cliffs. The routes are spread out between about one and fifteen minutes from the car.

ut_apetizer_wall.blurb: A wall of hard limestone sport routes in American Fork Canyon, filed under the Billboard crag at around 6,800 feet in the southern Wasatch. It holds everything on the crag that is not on the neighbouring grid-style wall, and its face starts out south-facing before swinging around to look south-southeast. Twenty bolted lines, with only a few at 5.10 or 5.11. The real weight is at 5.12 and 5.13, with one route in the low 5.14s, so this is a place for strong sport climbers. It is sunny, and carrying extra water is wise.

ut_peeler_face.blurb: The lower southeast face of Black Peeler Buttress in Little Cottonwood Canyon, in the Wasatch. The rock is steep and blank-looking, which is why the face is better known for aid lines and technical free climbs than for easy cragging. Of twenty routes, most are trad or aid, with free grades concentrated between 5.10 and 5.12 and a harder one just above. Most of the development dates to the 1980s. The approach is steep at the base, and the lines higher on the hill are a lot harder to reach through loose dirt and thick brush. It is a place for experienced multi-pitch parties.
